'''Sheldon Goldstein''' (born October 24, 1947, in [[Augusta, Georgia]])<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004.</ref> is an American theoretical physicist. He introduced the term "[[Bohmian mechanics]]".<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5rCtDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA198 |page=198 |title=David Bohm: A Life Dedicated to Understanding the Quantum World | isbn=9783030227159 | last1=Freire Jr. | first1=Olival | date=5 September 2019 | publisher=Springer }}</ref>

==Biography==
Goldstein graduated from [[Yeshiva University]] with a B.A. in 1969, a B.S. in 1971, and a Ph.D. in physics in 1973. His Ph.D. thesis, supervised by [[Joel Lebowitz]], is entitled ''Ergodic Theory and Infinite Systems'' <ref>{{cite web|author=Goldstein, Sheldon|title=Ergodic Theory and Infinite Systems|website=Yeshiva Academic Institutional Repository (YAIR)|url=https://repository.yu.edu/handle/20.500.12202/2181}} (doctoral dissertation)</ref> Since 1977 Goldstein has been a professor at [[Rutgers University]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Homepage of Sheldon Goldstein|website=Mathematics Department, Rutgers University|url=https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~oldstein/}} (with reprints & recent publications)</ref> His research deals with the foundations of quantum mechanics and, especially, theoretical developments of [[De Broglie–Bohm theory]]. His collaborators include Joel Lebowitz<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/BF01646030 |title=Ergodic properties of an infinite system of particles moving independently in a periodic field |date=1974 |last1=Goldstein |first1=Sheldon |last2=Lebowitz |first2=Joel L. |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=1–18 |bibcode=1974CMaPh..37....1G |s2cid=3560060 |url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1103859808 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/BF02046762 |title=A mechanical model of Brownian motion |date=1981 |last1=Dürr |first1=D. |last2=Goldstein |first2=S. |last3=Lebowitz |first3=J. L. |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=78 |issue=4 |pages=507–530 |bibcode=1981CMaPh..78..507D |s2cid=44757047 |url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1103908788 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and Detlef Dürr.<ref>{{cite book|author=Dürr, D.|author2=Goldstein, S.|author3=Tumulka, R.|author4=Zanghí, N.|title=Compendium of Quantum Physics |chapter=Bohmian Mechanics |year=2009|pages=47–55|location=Berlin; Heidelberg|publisher=Springer|doi=10.1007/978-3-540-70626-7_16|isbn=978-3-540-70622-9 }} [https://arxiv.org/pdf/0903.2601.pdf arXiv preprint]</ref> In a 1981 paper, Goldstein and [[Oliver Penrose]] described a new method of defining nonequilibrium entropy in statistical mechanics.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/BF01013304 |title=A nonequilibrium entropy for dynamical systems |date=1981 |last1=Goldstein |first1=S. |last2=Penrose |first2=O. |journal=Journal of Statistical Physics |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=325–343 |bibcode=1981JSP....24..325G |s2cid=123046920 }}</ref> Goldstein contributed the article ''Bohmian Mechanics'' to the ''[[Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]''.
<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://seop.illc.uva.nl/entries/qm-bohm/ |title=Bohmian Mechanics |date=26 October 2001 |last1=Goldstein |first1=Sheldon |website=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}}</ref>

For two academic years from 1973 to 1975, Goldstein was at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Sheldon Goldstein|website=Institute for Advanced Study (ias.edu)|date=9 December 2019 |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/sheldon-goldstein}}</ref> He is a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. He is a member of the board of governors of the John Bell Institute for the Foundations of Physics<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.johnbellinstitute.org/people/governors#h.p_73n-nMgiVda1 |title=John Bell Institute - Directors & Governors }}</ref> (founded by [[Tim Maudlin]]).

Sheldon Goldstein and [[Rebecca Goldstein|Rebecca Newberger Goldstein]], a novelist and philosopher, were married from 1969 to 1999, until they divorced. They are the parents of the novelist [[Yael Goldstein Love]]<ref>{{cite web|title=About Yael Goldstein-Love|website=yaelgoldsteinlove.com|url=https://www.yaelgoldsteinlove.com/about}}</ref> and the poet Danielle Blau.<ref>{{cite web|title=bio|website=Danielle Blau (danielleblau.com)|url=http://www.danielleblau.com/bio}}</ref>
